questions.stem: You are examining Mr Loh, 47, on the orthopaedic ward, day 5 after surgery for a right neck of femur fracture. He has sudden pleuritic chest pain, and his right calf has been sore, red and swollen since early this morning. You want to record the calf swelling objectively, as the Wells DVT criteria define it. How should you measure it?
options: Measure both ankles at the malleoli; any difference of more than 1 cm counts
Measure the right thigh 15 cm above the patella and compare with the admission measure
Measure both calves 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity; a difference over 3 cm counts
Dorsiflex the right foot with the knee extended and record any calf pain (Homans sign)
questions.why: Calf swelling in the Wells criteria is measured on both legs 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, and it counts when the affected calf is more than 3 cm bigger. Always examine and compare both legs when you suspect PE.
notes: Ankle swelling at the malleoli is not the validated measure. A 1 cm cut-off is too sensitive and picks up normal post-operative oedema.
The thigh is swollen after hip surgery anyway, and a single-leg measure compared over time is not the Wells criterion. The calf is where his symptoms are.
Homans sign is unreliable, has poor sensitivity and specificity, and is not part of any validated score. It should not be used to document a DVT.

questions.stem: Mr Loh, 47, weighs 98 kg and is day 5 after hip fracture surgery. He has been on prophylactic enoxaparin. CTPA shows bilateral lower lobe PE with no RV strain. BP is 128/78 and SpO2 is 94% on 2 L/min. Creatinine is 84, platelets 298 and Hb 118. The orthopaedic consultant agrees the bleeding risk is acceptable. Which anticoagulation plan is best?
options: Stop prophylactic enoxaparin; start enoxaparin 100 mg SC 12-hourly
Continue enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily and add enoxaparin 100 mg SC 12-hourly
Give alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours, then start an unfractionated heparin infusion
Withhold all anticoagulation and arrange an inferior vena cava filter
questions.why: A stable PE is treated with therapeutic anticoagulation: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly (about 100 mg for 98 kg, normal renal function). This replaces the prophylactic dose; it is not added to it. A PE provoked by surgery is treated for 3 months.
notes: Adding a therapeutic dose on top of the prophylactic dose doubles up the anticoagulation and raises the risk of bleeding, especially at a fresh surgical site.
Thrombolysis is for PE with shock. He is normotensive with no RV strain, and major surgery 5 days ago is a contraindication.
An IVC filter is only for patients who cannot be anticoagulated. His surgical team has agreed that anticoagulation is safe.

questions.stem: Mr Loh, 47, day 5 after hip surgery, has bilateral lower lobe PE on CTPA. He is breathing 28 times a minute with SpO2 91% on room air, and his RV is not dilated. A blood gas would be expected to show hypoxaemia with a low PaCO2. What is the main mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
options: Global alveolar hypoventilation from splinting of the chest by pleuritic pain
Thickening of the alveolar-capillary membrane that limits oxygen diffusion
Right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale from high right atrial pressure
V/Q mismatch, as blood is diverted to the lung regions that are still perfused
questions.why: In PE, emboli create dead space and push the cardiac output through the remaining lung, which then has a low V/Q ratio with a short transit time. This lowers PaO2. Hyperventilation clears CO2, so PaCO2 is usually low.
notes: Global hypoventilation would raise PaCO2. He is tachypnoeic and is expected to have a low PaCO2, so this cannot explain his hypoxaemia.
A diffusion defect happens in interstitial lung disease, not in acute vascular obstruction. His alveolar membrane is normal.
Shunting through a PFO needs raised right heart pressures, as in massive PE. His RV is not dilated and he has no strain.

questions.stem: Mr Loh, 47, day 5 after hip surgery, points to his right lower posterolateral chest. The pain is sharp, well localised and worse on deep inspiration. CTPA shows a small peripheral right lower lobe infarct with a small effusion. Which nerves carry this pain?
options: Vagal afferents from the visceral pleura over the infarcted lobe
Intercostal nerves supplying the costal parietal pleura
The phrenic nerve supplying the central diaphragmatic pleura
Cardiac sympathetic afferents entering the T1 to T4 cord segments
questions.why: The costal parietal pleura is supplied by somatic intercostal nerves. This is why inflammation over a peripheral infarct gives sharp pain that is well localised and pleuritic. The visceral pleura has no somatic pain fibres.
notes: The visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and is insensitive to pain. It cannot produce sharp, localised pleuritic pain.
Phrenic nerve pain from the central diaphragmatic pleura is referred to the shoulder tip (C3 to C5), not the lower posterolateral chest wall.
Cardiac visceral afferents produce diffuse central pain, like the pain of ACS, and it is poorly localised. It does not change with breathing.
